title: Variables
explanation: A variable is a name bound to a value in memory. Python is dynamically typed, so you don't declare a type - it is inferred from the value you assign. Names must start with a letter or underscore and are case-sensitive.
code_example:
age = 21
name = "Agrim"
is_student = True
print(age, name, is_student)

keywords: data types int float str bool list tuple dict set
title: Built-in Data Types
explanation: Core built-in types: int, float, complex, str, bool, list, tuple, dict, set, frozenset, bytes, and NoneType. Use type(x) to check a value's type.
code_example:
x = 10          # int
y = 3.14        # float
name = "hi"     # str
flag = True     # bool
items = [1,2,3] # list
point = (1,2)   # tuple
person = {"a":1} # dict
uniq = {1,2,3}  # set
print(type(x), type(name))

title: Operators
explanation: Arithmetic: + - * / // % **. Comparison: == != > < >= <=. Logical: and or not. Bitwise: & | ^ ~ << >>. // is floor division, ** is exponent.

title: Conditionals (if/elif/else)
explanation: Conditionals run code based on a boolean expression. Python uses indentation (not braces) to define blocks - be consistent with spaces.

keywords: loop for while range break continue
title: Loops (for / while)
explanation: `for` iterates over an iterable (list, range, string...). `while` repeats while a condition is true. `break` exits a loop, `continue` skips to the next iteration.

keywords: function def parameters arguments return default args kwargs
title: Functions
explanation: Define reusable code with `def`. Parameters can have default values, and you can accept variable args (*args) and keyword args (**kwargs).

title: Lambda Functions
explanation: A lambda is a small anonymous function: `lambda args: expression`. Useful for short throwaway functions, e.g. as a `key=` for sorted().
code_example:
square = lambda x: x * x
print(square(5))

names = ["Bob", "al", "Charlie"]
print(sorted(names, key=lambda s: len(s)))

keywords: list comprehension dict comprehension set comprehension
title: Comprehensions
explanation: Comprehensions build lists/dicts/sets in one concise line, often faster and more readable than an equivalent for-loop with append().

keywords: string str methods slicing format f-string
title: Strings
explanation: Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Slicing: s[start:stop:step]. Common methods: split, join, strip, replace, upper/lower, find. f-strings embed expressions: f'{value}'.
code_example:
s = "  Hello, World!  "
print(s.strip().lower())
print(s[2:7])
parts = "a,b,c".split(",")
print("-".join(parts))
name = "Agrim"
print(f"Hi {name}, len={len(name)}")

keywords: list methods append pop insert remove sort slicing
title: Lists
explanation: Lists are ordered, mutable sequences. Key methods: append, extend, insert, pop, remove, sort, reverse. Slicing works the same as strings.
code_example:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
nums.append(9)
nums.sort()
print(nums)
print(nums[1:4])
nums.remove(1)
print(nums)

keywords: dictionary dict keys values items get update
title: Dictionaries
explanation: Dicts store key-value pairs (insertion-ordered since 3.7). Use .get(key, default) to avoid KeyError, .items()/.keys()/.values() to iterate.

title: Tuples
explanation: Tuples are ordered and immutable. Great for fixed collections and for unpacking multiple return values.
code_example:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)

def minmax(nums):
    return min(nums), max(nums)

lo, hi = minmax([4,1,9,2])
print(lo, hi)

title: Sets
explanation: Sets are unordered collections of unique items. Support union (|), intersection (&), difference (-), and symmetric_difference (^).

keywords: exception try except finally error handling raise
title: Exception Handling
explanation: Wrap risky code in try/except. Use `finally` for cleanup that always runs, and `raise` to signal your own errors. Catch specific exceptions rather than a bare `except:`.

title: Custom Exceptions
explanation: Create your own exception types by subclassing Exception. This makes error handling more precise in larger programs.

title: Classes & Objects
explanation: A class is a blueprint for objects. `__init__` is the constructor, `self` refers to the current instance.

keywords: inheritance super parent child class extend
title: Inheritance
explanation: A subclass inherits attributes/methods from a parent class. Use super() to call the parent's implementation.

title: Polymorphism
explanation: Different classes can implement the same method name differently. Code that calls the method doesn't need to know the exact class.

title: Encapsulation
explanation: Python uses naming conventions for access control: `_protected` (by convention) and `__private` (name-mangled). `@property` exposes controlled getters/setters.

title: Decorators
explanation: A decorator wraps a function to add behaviour without modifying its code. Use functools.wraps to preserve the original function's metadata.

title: Generators & Iterators
explanation: Generators produce values lazily with `yield`, saving memory versus building a full list. Any object with __iter__/__next__ is an iterator.

keywords: magic methods dunder str repr eq len
title: Magic / Dunder Methods
explanation: Special methods like __str__, __repr__, __eq__, __len__ let your objects work with built-in functions and operators.

keywords: file open read write with context manager
title: File Handling
explanation: Use `with open(path, mode) as f:` so the file is closed automatically. Modes: 'r' read, 'w' write (overwrite), 'a' append, 'rb'/'wb' binary.
code_example:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello file!\n")

with open("notes.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()
print(content)

keywords: module import package pip install venv virtual environment
title: Modules, Packages & pip
explanation: A module is a .py file; a package is a folder of modules with __init__.py. `pip install <name>` installs third-party packages. Use a virtual environment per project: `python -m venv venv` then activate it.
code_example:
# terminal commands
python -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows
source venv/bin/activate    # macOS/Linux
pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt

keywords: regex re module pattern match search findall sub
title: Regex Basics (re module)
explanation: The `re` module does pattern matching. re.match checks the start of a string, re.search finds anywhere, re.findall returns all matches, re.sub replaces matches.
code_example:
import re

text = "Call me at 987-654-3210 or 123-456-7890"
pattern = r"\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}"
print(re.findall(pattern, text))
print(re.sub(pattern, "[hidden]", text))

title: Regex Groups & Compiling
explanation: Parentheses create capture groups. Use (?P<name>...) for named groups. re.compile() precompiles a pattern for reuse/performance.
code_example:
import re
pattern = re.compile(r"(?P<user>[\w.]+)@(?P<domain>[\w.]+)")
m = pattern.search("contact: agrim@example.com")
print(m.group("user"), m.group("domain"))

keywords: regex email validation phone validation common patterns
title: Common Regex Patterns
explanation: Handy reusable patterns for validation tasks. Note: for real email validation, a simple regex is a heuristic, not a full RFC check.
code_example:
import re
EMAIL = r"^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,}$"
PHONE_IN = r"^[6-9]\d{9}$"
print(bool(re.match(EMAIL, "agrim@lbsim.in")))
print(bool(re.match(PHONE_IN, "9876543210")))

title: NumPy Arrays
explanation: numpy.ndarray is a fast, fixed-type, multi-dimensional array - the base of numerical Python. Much faster than plain Python lists for math.
code_example:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
b = a.reshape(2, 2)
print(b)
print(a * 2)
print(a.sum(), a.mean())

title: Pandas DataFrames
explanation: pandas.DataFrame is a labeled 2D table, built on numpy. Read data with pd.read_csv(), inspect with .head()/.info(), filter with boolean masks.
code_example:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["A", "B"], "score": [80, 92]})
print(df.head())
print(df[df["score"] > 85])

title: Starting a Django Project
explanation: Django is installed via pip and scaffolded with django-admin. A project can contain multiple apps. manage.py runs project-level commands.
code_example:
# terminal commands
pip install django
django-admin startproject mysite
cd mysite
python manage.py startapp blog
python manage.py runserver

title: Django Models
explanation: Models define your database schema as Python classes in models.py. Each class attribute maps to a table column via a Field type.
code_example:
# blog/models.py
from django.db import models

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    content = models.TextField()
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

title: Django Migrations
explanation: Migrations sync your models with the database schema. Run makemigrations after changing models, then migrate to apply them.
code_example:
# terminal commands
python manage.py makemigrations
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py createsuperuser

keywords: django view views.py request response render
title: Django Views
explanation: A view is a Python function (or class) that takes a request and returns a response, often rendering an HTML template.

title: Django URLs
explanation: urls.py maps URL paths to views. Each app usually has its own urls.py included from the project's main urls.py.
code_example:
# blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.post_list, name="post_list"),
]

keywords: django orm queryset filter get all objects
title: Django ORM Queries
explanation: Model.objects is the manager used to query the database: .all(), .filter(), .get(), .exclude(), .order_by() build QuerySets lazily.
code_example:
from blog.models import Post

Post.objects.all()
Post.objects.filter(title__icontains="django")
Post.objects.get(id=1)
Post.objects.order_by("-created_at")[:5]

title: Django Forms
explanation: Django Forms handle input validation and HTML rendering. ModelForm auto-generates a form from a model.
code_example:
# blog/forms.py
from django import forms
from .models import Post

class PostForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Post
        fields = ["title", "content"]

title: Django Admin
explanation: Django's built-in admin gives a ready-made UI for managing your models. Register models in admin.py to expose them.
code_example:
# blog/admin.py
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Post

admin.site.register(Post)

keywords: django template templates render html jinja
title: Django Templates
explanation: Templates are HTML files with Django Template Language tags ({{ }} for variables, {% %} for logic) rendered by views.
code_example:
{% for post in posts %}
  • {{ post.title }}
    • {% endfor %}

keywords: django rest framework drf api serializer
title: Django REST Framework Basics
explanation: DRF (installed separately: pip install djangorestframework) adds Serializers (convert models <-> JSON) and API Views/ViewSets for building REST APIs on top of Django.
code_example:
# serializers.py
from rest_framework import serializers
from .models import Post

class PostSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Post
        fields = "__all__"
